title: At someone's home
goal: Be a good guest and a good host: arrive, accept and refuse food the polite way, offer to help, pitch in with chores, stay the night — and talk about how things used to be at home.
intro:
Sooner or later a friend says **घरी ये ना** 'come over'. A Marathi home has its own small rituals: shoes off at the door, the host's **आग्रह** (insisting you eat more), the guest's polite 'no' that isn't always a no, and the friend's mum who becomes **काकू** the moment you walk in.

This unit gives you the words for all of that, plus three pieces of grammar: how to offer, insist and decline gracefully, how to ask **'should I…?'** (करू का?, करावं का?), and the **'used to'** form (मी जायचो) that every conversation about family and childhood needs.

grammar.title: 'Used to': मी जायचो, ती यायची
grammar.body:
For things that happened regularly in the past — childhood, how life was before — Marathi has a special **habitual past**: stem + **आय** + the endings of the past tense.

मी जा**यचो** (m) / जा**यचे** (f) — I used to go
तू जा**यचास** / जा**यचीस** — you used to go
तो जा**यचा** · ती जा**यची** · ते (n) जा**यचं**
आम्ही जा**यचो** · तुम्ही जा**यचात**
ते जा**यचे** · त्या जा**यच्या**

Vowel stems take -य-: खा → खायचो, पि → **प्यायचो**, ये → **यायचो**, दे → **द्यायचो**, घे → **घ्यायचो**, अस → असायचो.

**No ergative here.** Even with an object, the verb agrees with the **subject**: तो रोज पेपर **वाचायचा** (not *त्याने… वाचला*), आई रोज पोळ्या **करायची**.

**Negative:** add नाही with its person ending: मी जायचो **नाही**, ते यायचे **नाहीत**.

**The trap:** this looks like the 'need to' form (मला जायचं आहे). The difference is the subject: **मी** जायचो = I used to go; **मला** जायचं होतं = I was supposed to go.

**Being used to** something is a different idea: **मला सवय आहे** 'I'm used to it'; मला लवकर उठायची सवय आहे 'I'm used to getting up early'.

grammar.title: Offering, insisting and saying no nicely
grammar.body:
Food at someone's home comes with a little dance called **आग्रह** — the host insists, the guest refuses, the host insists again. Knowing the steps makes you a good guest.

**Offering:**
- polite imperative + **ना**: बसा **ना**, घ्या **ना** 'do have some'
- **-णार का?** / **काय घेणार?**: चहा **घेणार का?** 'will you have tea?' — the everyday way to offer
- **अजून**: **अजून** थोडं घ्या 'have some more'
- add **हो** for warmth (very common with elders): घ्या **हो**, बसा **हो**

**Insisting (आग्रह):** एवढंच? 'that's all?' · थोडंच आहे 'it's only a little' · अर्धी तरी घे 'at least have half'.

**Declining:** **नको** + a reason sounds kind; नको on its own can sound blunt. नको, पोट भरलं · नको, खरंच खूप झालं · **पुरे** / **बस** 'enough' · **राहू दे** 'leave it' (Unit 18).

**Accepting:** बरं, थोडंसं · **अर्धाच** 'just half' · चालेल 'that'll do'.

**How it works in practice:** the first 'no' is often just politeness and the host will offer again. If you really don't want more, say so twice with a reason, and cover your plate with your hand. Leaving a little food on your plate is fine; taking more and leaving it is not.

examples.en: Go on, take some, don't be shy.

grammar.title: 'Should I…?': करू का? and करावं का?
grammar.body:
There are two ways to ask 'should I?', and they're not quite the same.

**stem + ऊ + का?** — offering or asking permission ('shall I? / may I?'), which you met in Unit 18: मी भांडी **घासू** का? 'shall I do the dishes?', मी इथे **बसू** का? 'can I sit here?'. This is the one you'll use most as a guest.

**stem + आवं + का?** — asking for advice or about the rules ('should I? / ought I?'): मी काय **आणावं**? 'what should I bring?', मी त्यांना काका **म्हणावं** का? 'should I call him Kaka?'. Forms: कर → करावं, ये → यावं, जा → जावं, घे → घ्यावं, दे → द्यावं.
In careful speech the -आवं form agrees with an object like an adjective (-आवा m, -आवी f, -आवं n, -आवे m pl, -आव्या f pl): चपला कुठे **ठेवाव्या**? Most people simply use -आवं everywhere.

**'What do we do now?'** — in speech the -आयचं form is also used this way: आता काय **करायचं**? · कुठे **बसायचं**? 'where are we supposed to sit?'

**Answers:** हो, कर ना / करा ना 'sure, go ahead' · नको, राहू दे 'no, leave it' · काही नको, फक्त या 'don't bring anything, just come'.

examples.en: Should I take my shoes off here?
So what do we do now?
Shall I drop you at the station?

dialogue.title: Dinner at Sai's
dialogue.setting: Rohan goes to his friend Sai's flat in Kothrud, Pune, for dinner. Sai's mother — Kaku to Rohan — has cooked.

lines.en: Mum, dinner's ready, right? I'm starving.

lines.speaker: Kaku
lines.en: That's all? At least have half.

lines.roman: āī, hā lahānpaṇī paṇ asaṃts mhaṇāytsā, āṇi mag tīn poḷyā khāytsā!
lines.en: Mum, he used to say that as a kid too — and then eat three chapatis!

lines.speaker: Rohan
lines.native: बरं, अर्धी. पण भाजी खूप मस्त झालीय, काकू!
lines.roman: baraṃ, ardhī. paṇ bhājī khūp mast dzhālīy, kākū!
lines.en: OK, half. But the sabzi is amazing, Kaku!

lines.speaker: Kaku
lines.native: अजिबात नाही! तू पाहुणा आहेस. आणि आज इथेच राहा, उशीर झालाय.
lines.roman: ajibāt nāhī! tū pāhuṇā āhes. āṇi ādz ithets rāhā, ushīr dzhālāy.
lines.en: Absolutely not! You're a guest. And stay over tonight, it's late.

culture: Shoes come off at the door — look for the pile of चपला outside or just inside. Your friend's parents are **काका** and **काकू** (in some families आई-बाबा too), and you use **तुम्ही** with them even if they call you **तू** from the first minute. Bringing something is a nice touch — sweets, fruit, a box of पेढे — and the host will always say **उगाच कशाला आणलंस?** 'why did you bother?'. Expect to be offered **चहा** and, in Maharashtra, very often **पोहे** or उपमा; it's polite to accept at least a little. Many homes have a **देवघर**, a small shrine; don't put your feet towards it or step over things placed there. On festivals or when meeting a friend's grandparents, younger people often **touch their feet** (पाया पडणे) — you won't be expected to, but it's warmly received. Puneri hosts are the butt of affectionate jokes for asking 'चहा घेणार **ना**?' in a tone that expects 'no'; Mumbai and village hosts are the opposite and will refill your plate without asking. When you leave, don't say जातो 'I'm going' — say **येतो** / **येते** 'I'll come (again)', and the host replies **सावकाश जा** or **पुन्हा नक्की या**.

tip.title: करू का? करावं का? — should I…?
tip.body:
- **stem + ऊ + का?** offers or asks permission: मी आत **येऊ** का? · पाणी **देऊ** का? 'shall I get you water?'
- **stem + आवं + का?** asks what you ought to do: मी काय **आणावं**? 'what should I bring?' · मी त्यांना काका **म्हणावं** का?
- Answer: हो, कर ना / करा ना · नको, राहू दे.

tip.title: घ्या ना · नको, पोट भरलं — offering and declining
tip.body:
- Offer with **घ्या ना**, **घेणार का?**, **अजून थोडं**; add **हो** for warmth: घ्या हो.
- Decline with **नको + a reason**: नको, पोट भरलं · **पुरे** / **बस** 'enough'.
- Accept with **थोडंसं**, **अर्धाच**, **चालेल**.
- The first 'no' is often just politeness — expect the host to insist (आग्रह).

tip.title: मी जायचो — I used to go
tip.body:
- **Used to** = stem + **आय** + past endings: मी जा**यचो** (m) / जा**यचे** (f), तू जा**यचास**, तो जा**यचा**, ती जा**यची**, आम्ही जा**यचो**, ते जा**यचे**.
- No -ने and no object agreement: तो पेपर **वाचायचा**.
- Vowel stems: ये → **यायचो**, पि → **प्यायचो**.
- Don't mix it up with **मला** जायचं होतं 'I was supposed to go'.

sentences.en: As kids we used to go to Grandma's in the holidays.
